title: Longview Wants Input on Fourth Street Before a $200,000 Corridor Plan Takes Shape
thumbnailMessage: Longview wants Fourth Street input Thursday
summary: Longview’s MPO is studying Fourth Street between Loop 281 and Hawkins Parkway. A public open house is set for Thursday, Aug. 13, before recommendations are finalized.
content:
Longview residents have a chance this week to influence a transportation plan before its recommendations harden into a list of future projects. The city has scheduled a Fourth Street Corridor Study open house for Thursday, Aug. 13, from 5 to 7 p.m. at Maude Cobb Convention Center, 100 Grand Boulevard. The notice says City Council members may attend.

The meeting is not a vote to widen Fourth Street, approve construction or spend a new road-building appropriation. It is a public-input step in a planning study led by the Longview Metropolitan Planning Organization and the City of Longview. That distinction matters: residents should not be told that a specific project has been chosen when the city’s own scope calls for data collection, traffic modeling, alternatives and public feedback first.

The public record does establish the scale of the study. The city’s request for qualifications set a consultant-services budget of up to $200,000 and a completion deadline before Sept. 30, 2027. The document says the work is also funded through the Federal Highway Administration and Federal Transit Administration. That is planning money, not a $200,000 construction budget. Any later construction proposal would need its own cost estimate, funding source and public approvals.

The core study area is Fourth Street between East Loop 281 and Hawkins Parkway, including its connections with State Highway Spur 502, also known as Judson Road, and U.S. 259, or Eastman Road. The city describes the area as highly developed and increasingly commercial. Its procurement packet names Home Depot, Lowe’s, Sam’s Club, Walmart Supercenter, other retail and food businesses, and Longview High School as major traffic generators. It calls the area one of the region’s most traveled each day.

That mix makes the corridor more than a question of how quickly cars move. Students, school employees, shoppers, workers, delivery drivers, transit riders, pedestrians, bicyclists, emergency vehicles and nearby residents all use the same network. A change that improves one movement can create a new delay or safety problem somewhere else. The study should show those tradeoffs rather than hide them inside a single congestion score.

The city’s scope is broad enough to produce a useful record. It directs the consultant to gather traffic volumes, crash reports, land-use and zoning data, existing plans and geographic information. It calls for review of current traffic operations and crash history at the corridor’s major intersections. It also requires traffic simulations, volume-to-capacity analysis and testing of alternative intersection or roadway configurations.

Public engagement is part of the contract, not an optional courtesy. The scope calls for workshops, surveys or interviews and requires the consultant to collect and summarize feedback from residents, businesses and partner agencies. That means Thursday’s comments should leave an auditable trail. The final report should identify what people raised, how many participants responded, which ideas changed the analysis and which requests were rejected with an explanation.

Residents can make the open house more productive by asking for the baseline before debating a preferred design. The city should display recent daily and peak-hour traffic counts, turning movements at key intersections, crash locations by severity and type, school arrival and dismissal patterns, transit stops, sidewalk gaps, bicycle conditions and known access problems at commercial driveways. Without a common set of facts, the loudest complaint can crowd out the most serious risk.

Crash data need particular care. A map of dots is not enough. The study should separate fatal and serious-injury crashes from minor property-damage events, identify patterns involving left turns, rear-end collisions or vulnerable road users, and explain the years covered. If a location looks dangerous because it carries far more traffic than another, the analysis should include an exposure rate as well as a raw count. Personal information about crash victims should remain protected.

The consultant is also expected to examine multimodal access. That phrase should produce specific, testable options: continuous sidewalks, safe crossings, curb ramps, bus-stop access, bicycle connections and designs that comply with the Americans with Disabilities Act. Residents with disabilities, parents moving children, older adults and people who do not drive should be able to see how an alternative affects an actual trip, not simply read that accessibility was considered.

Business access deserves the same precision. Fourth Street supports a large commercial district, and changes to medians, driveways or signal timing can affect deliveries and customer routes. Businesses should identify where queues block entrances, where turning vehicles create conflicts and when trucks need access. But private convenience should not automatically override public safety. The final recommendation should state which access changes were modeled and why each was accepted or rejected.

The procurement record also calls for rough cost estimates, implementation phases and possible funding sources. That is where accountability becomes concrete. Every recommended project should carry a planning-level price range, an explanation of who would own it, a likely funding program, maintenance responsibility and a realistic sequence. A wish list without costs is not a plan; a cost without an identified payer is not a commitment.

Longview should publish the consultant contract and name the project team if it has not already done so in an easily searchable place. The public should be able to compare the executed agreement with the original scope, see the not-to-exceed amount, identify any subcontractors and follow invoices or progress reports. The request for qualifications is closed, but a closed solicitation should lead to an open contract record.

The study’s funding structure adds another reason for transparency. Federal transportation dollars come with planning and civil-rights requirements, while the city’s own packet notes that Longview budget authority operates by fiscal year. The final report should distinguish money already authorized for consultant work from any future local match or capital request. Residents should not have to infer those amounts from several budget documents.

Thursday’s format should also allow participation beyond the two-hour room. The city can post display boards, maps and a survey online; provide a deadline for written comments; offer an accessible format; and publish a contact for residents who cannot attend. A sign-in sheet may help count participation, but people should not be required to surrender unnecessary personal information to comment on a public road.

Elected officials have a role even though the open house is not a council vote. Council members can ask whether the outreach reached apartment residents, school families, transit users, businesses and people living near the corridor—not only organized groups. They can insist that the draft alternatives return to the public before final adoption. And when a capital proposal eventually appears, they can tie their votes to the published evidence.

The MPO should establish milestones now: existing-conditions report, alternatives analysis, draft recommendation, cost and phasing plan, public-comment summary, board action and any City Council action. A deadline of September 2027 leaves enough time for several meaningful checkpoints. It should not become an excuse for a long period of public silence followed by a finished plan.

Residents do not need to arrive Thursday with an engineering solution. The most useful contribution may be a repeated experience: a crossing that feels unsafe, a queue that appears only during school dismissal, a bus stop that cannot be reached by sidewalk, a signal phase that traps a turning driver or a driveway where sight distance is poor. Specific location, time and direction make an observation easier to test.

Longview’s stated objective is to improve circulation, safety and access for all users. Those goals can conflict, and the study will earn trust only by showing how it weighs them. The $200,000 public investment should buy more than a polished map. It should buy a shared factual record, alternatives the community can compare, costs taxpayers can understand and a recommendation that elected officials can defend in public.

The immediate action is straightforward: the open house is Thursday, Aug. 13, from 5 to 7 p.m. at Maude Cobb Convention Center. The larger accountability test comes afterward. Longview should publish what it heard, what the data show, what the consultant proposes and what each future decision would cost before asking residents to accept a redesigned Fourth Street.
